-description: Decompose batches of RHAISTRAT strategies into implementation epic DAGs. Accepts explicit IDs or a JQL query. Non-interactive.

+description: Decompose batches of RHAISTRAT strategies into implementation epic DAGs. Accepts explicit IDs or a JQL query. Use when decomposing RHAISTRAT strategies into epics, or when asked to run the epic-decompose pipeline on a strategy or batch. Non-interactive.
- Priority inheritance: prerequisite epic inherits the highest priority of all HLRs it transitively enables
- An epic blocking all P0 work is implicitly P0

-- Priority split: when an epic maps to HLRs at multiple priority levels, check whether the lower-priority HLRs represent distinct, deferrable features. A feature is "distinct and deferrable" only when it could ship as its own epic with independent user value AND does not share data structures, UI surfaces, or API endpoints with the P0 work. If yes, split them into separate epics by priority so each can be planned independently. If the lower-priority HLR is incidental to the P0 work (error handling, doc coverage, config override that falls out of the same implementation) or is tightly coupled to the same implementation surface, keep it bundled — splitting tightly coupled work creates duplication and artificial boundaries.

+- Priority split: when an epic maps to HLRs at multiple priority levels, check whether the lower-priority HLRs represent distinct, deferrable features. A feature is "distinct and deferrable" only when it could ship as its own epic with independent user value AND does not share data structures, UI surfaces, or API endpoints with the P0 work. If yes, split them into separate epics by priority so each can be planned independently. If the lower-priority HLR is incidental to the P0 work (error handling, doc coverage, config override that falls out of the same implementation) or is tightly coupled to the same implementation surface, keep it bundled — splitting tightly coupled work creates duplication and artificial boundaries. **When you keep a lower-priority HLR bundled in a higher-priority epic, record the judgment in the HLR Traceability Matrix row itself:** mark the row's epic entry `(bundled)` and put the coupling rationale inline in the row's Notes (shared surface, why the HLR is not independently deferrable, what splitting would cost — e.g. two passes over the same call sites) — or, equivalently, carry a self-contained note that states the full rationale on its own. A bare pointer with no rationale ("bundled with P0 work per the rule above") is the defect shape: the bundling judgment must be readable from the matrix row or the note without hunting for the rule.

- **Redundant / overlapping HLRs — consolidate, never split:** strategies merged from multiple sources sometimes state one capability twice in different words (e.g. "select two or more runs and view their parameters and metrics side by side" and "a diff view highlighting which parameters and metrics changed between two selected runs" — the diff view is a presentation mode of the same comparison surface over the same run data). When two HLRs describe the same data structure, UI surface, or API endpoint for the same component and team — one a restatement or presentation mode of the other — they are ONE capability: cover both with a single epic whose HLR Traceability lists both HLR ids, at the higher of the two priorities. Do not split them into separate epics by priority label: on a shared surface a P0/P1 pair is redundant wording, not a deferral signal, and splitting produces two epics building the same surface plus an artificial serialization edge between them — a boundary violation even when the second epic only extends the first's surface.

- `docs-authoring` priority exception: `docs-authoring` epics are exempt from priority inheritance. They do not push their priority upstream to the implementations they depend on. Instead, derive their priority from the strategy frontmatter `priority` field: Critical→P0, Major→P1, Normal/Minor/Undefined→P2. If the field is missing or empty, default to P2.

- **Work-product type boundaries**: code implementation, content authoring (sample notebooks, tutorials, curated examples), and documentation are different kinds of work — they require different skills, different review criteria, and produce different PR review cycles. An epic that mixes code implementation with content authoring should be split even if the same team owns both. **Exception — incidental documentation touch-ups:** updating captions, screenshots, or references that fall out of a code change (no new content authored) is not a separate work stream — fold it into the originating epic as scope/acceptance criteria rather than a standalone `docs-authoring` epic. Only substantive content/documentation authoring (new tutorials, sample notebooks, curated examples, new or rewritten doc topics), or a strategy with `Documentation Support: Yes`, warrants a separate epic.

These axes take precedence when deciding where to draw epic boundaries within a component. Step 4 may additionally split by priority when features are genuinely deferrable — but the initial boundary structure should come from architecture and work-product type, not from walking down the HLR list. Never split such that two epics must build the same data structure, UI surface, or API endpoint independently.

+   **Shared-surface enforcement deliverables divide per surface, not per work type.** When a strategy calls for an enforcement or verification deliverable that applies across the same surfaces being converted (a lint rule or CI check over converted code, a validation harness over migrated components, a convention check over refactored files), do NOT extract it into its own standalone epic next to the per-surface implementation epics — that carves one logical change into a work-type epic and leaves each implementation epic's slice incomplete without it. Instead, each surface epic's Scope and Acceptance Criteria include the deliverable's slice for its own surface (the epic that converts a surface also authors and verifies the rule's coverage of that surface). Record the division in the summary's DAG Justification as part of the parallel non-edge rationale. Worked example: a strategy converting two binaries of one repo and adding a repo-wide structured-log lint rule → the manager-binary epic delivers and verifies the lint coverage for the manager binary's code paths, the cloudmanager epic does the same for its own; no standalone lint epic. This division also keeps each epic inside the epic-size guideline instead of stacking the whole shared deliverable onto one epic or fragmenting the sweep.
- Priority inversions (P0/P1/P2 inconsistent with technical complexity/reliability)
- Scope traps: ACs implying infrastructure that doesn't exist, contradictions between out-of-scope items and NFRs, storage beyond design intent
+When an epic's strategy-derived effort estimate exceeds the ~2-week epic guideline, resolve it in this order BEFORE considering any split:

+1. **Shared-surface deliverable stacked on per-surface work** → apply the Step 5 per-surface division rule (the surface epics each take the deliverable's slice). This usually brings every epic under the guideline.

+2. **Still one logical change over an enumerated surface** (a single mechanical sweep — one conversion or addition applied uniformly to every file in an enumerated set, where the strategy's own work breakdown presents it as one work item): keep the epic intact — splitting it forces multiple passes over the same files and fragments one logical change. Record in Health Warnings (a) the estimate and why the sweep is one logical change, and (b) a **concrete conditional re-split trigger**: the measurable condition under which the epic should be re-split (e.g. the validated audit of affected call sites materially exceeding the strategy's estimate, or capacity constraints requiring independently schedulable units). A size note that only flags the overage "for planning awareness" is an unmanaged overage — the trigger is what makes keeping it a recorded, managed trade-off.

+3. **Heterogeneous work bundled into one epic** (multiple logical changes or distinct work streams that happened to land together) → split along the architectural seam, as the boundary rules already provide.
+Never split a one-logical-change sweep by work type (lint rule vs. conversion, tests vs. code) — that is shape 2, not shape 3.
- **0**: P0 HLR(s) missing from epic set, or traceability matrix absent.

-Check: Read the strategy's HLR list. For each HLR, verify it appears in at least one epic's "HLR Traceability" section. Verify priority inheritance — an epic blocking all P0 work must be P0. Exception: `docs-authoring` epics are exempt from priority inheritance; their priority derives from the strategy's Jira priority (Critical→P0, Major→P1, Normal/Minor/Undefined→P2), not from the implementations they depend on. Do not flag a `docs-authoring` epic's dependency on a lower-priority implementation as a priority inheritance violation. Check for priority collapse — if an epic maps to HLRs at multiple priority levels and the lower-priority HLRs are distinct deferrable features (not incidental polish on the P0 work), they should be in separate epics so they can be planned independently. Priority collapse with deferrable features is a major issue — the ability to defer work independently is a planning requirement that overrides boundary convenience. **Exception: triaged strategies.** If `triage: below-threshold` or `triage: docs-only`, the single-epic output is correct by design (Step 0 takes precedence over priority-split logic). Do not flag priority collapse on a triaged strategy — all HLRs are bundled intentionally.

+Check: Read the strategy's HLR list. For each HLR, verify it appears in at least one epic's "HLR Traceability" section. Verify priority inheritance — an epic blocking all P0 work must be P0. Exception: `docs-authoring` epics are exempt from priority inheritance; their priority derives from the strategy's Jira priority (Critical→P0, Major→P1, Normal/Minor/Undefined→P2), not from the implementations they depend on. Do not flag a `docs-authoring` epic's dependency on a lower-priority implementation as a priority inheritance violation. Check for priority collapse — if an epic maps to HLRs at multiple priority levels and the lower-priority HLRs are distinct deferrable features (not incidental polish on the P0 work), they should be in separate epics so they can be planned independently. Priority collapse with deferrable features is a major issue — the ability to defer work independently is a planning requirement that overrides boundary convenience. A lower-priority HLR is NOT "distinct and deferrable" when it shares the implementation surface with the P0 work (the same files, call sites, or endpoints the P0 HLRs edit): splitting it out forces multiple passes over the same surface and creates an artificial serialization boundary — in that case verify instead that the bundling is recorded with its rationale in the HLR Traceability Matrix row (a `(bundled)` marker with inline rationale, or a self-contained note); a bare pointer with no rationale is a minor issue with the correction "record the coupling rationale in the matrix row". **Exception: triaged strategies.** If `triage: below-threshold` or `triage: docs-only`, the single-epic output is correct by design (Step 0 takes precedence over priority-split logic). Do not flag priority collapse on a triaged strategy — all HLRs are bundled intentionally.
- **0**: Epics violate the component/team boundary rule (work for different teams bundled into one epic), or an epic is clearly oversized (multiple sprints of work).

-Check: For each epic, verify component and team fields. Look for epics that bundle work across multiple components or teams. **Also check for scope duplication across sibling epics:** compare the scope sections and acceptance criteria of all epics. If two or more epics independently build the same data structure, UI surface, API endpoint, or component (e.g., both create a benchmark list with status indicators, or both implement log viewing against the same endpoint), that is a major issue — it means the boundary was drawn incorrectly and the epics should be merged or re-split along a different axis. Minor incidental overlap (e.g., both epics mention the same config value) is not duplication. **A split that puts two presentation modes of ONE surface in two epics is duplication even though neither epic rebuilds the other's work** — e.g., a P0 epic building a side-by-side comparison view and a P1 epic building a diff view of the same data for the same team: the diff view is a thin increment on the first epic's surface, not an independent deliverable, and the correct shape is ONE epic whose HLR Traceability lists both HLRs. A priority-label difference (P0 vs P1) on the same surface is redundant requirement wording, not a boundary — flag the split as a major issue. **Also check for work-product type mixing:** if a single epic bundles code implementation with content authoring (sample notebooks, tutorials, curated examples), flag as a major issue — these are different kinds of work with different review criteria and should be separate epics even when owned by the same team.

+Check: For each epic, verify component and team fields. Look for epics that bundle work across multiple components or teams. **Size check — classify before flagging.** When an epic appears to exceed the ~2-week guideline, determine which shape it is before demanding anything:
+- **Heterogeneous monolith** (multiple logical changes or distinct work streams bundled into one epic) → major issue; demand a split along the architectural seam.

+- **One-logical-change sweep over an enumerated surface** (a single mechanical conversion/addition applied uniformly to an enumerated file or component set, presented by the strategy as one work item) → the compliant shape is a Health Warning carrying a concrete conditional re-split trigger. If the trigger is present, do NOT demand a split and do not dock the criterion — record at most a watch note. If it is absent, flag a **minor** issue with the correction "record a concrete re-split trigger in Health Warnings" — never demand a split of a single sweep, and never propose a split that cannot bring the epic under the guideline (an un-actionable split demand causes revise churn without resolving the size flag).

+- **Shared-surface enforcement deliverable extracted into its own epic** while per-surface implementation epics also exist (a standalone lint-rule/tooling/validation epic next to the epics whose surfaces the rule covers) → **minor** issue with the correction "divide the deliverable per surface into the consuming epics" — the boundary was drawn by work type and fragments one logical change; merging it back per surface is the fix, not further splitting.

+**Also check for scope duplication across sibling epics:** compare the scope sections and acceptance criteria of all epics. If two or more epics independently build the same data structure, UI surface, API endpoint, or component (e.g., both create a benchmark list with status indicators, or both implement log viewing against the same endpoint), that is a major issue — it means the boundary was drawn incorrectly and the epics should be merged or re-split along a different axis. Minor incidental overlap (e.g., both epics mention the same config value) is not duplication. **A split that puts two presentation modes of ONE surface in two epics is duplication even though neither epic rebuilds the other's work** — e.g., a P0 epic building a side-by-side comparison view and a P1 epic building a diff view of the same data for the same team: the diff view is a thin increment on the first epic's surface, not an independent deliverable, and the correct shape is ONE epic whose HLR Traceability lists both HLRs. A priority-label difference (P0 vs P1) on the same surface is redundant requirement wording, not a boundary — flag the split as a major issue. **Also check for work-product type mixing:** if a single epic bundles code implementation with content authoring (sample notebooks, tutorials, curated examples), flag as a major issue — these are different kinds of work with different review criteria and should be separate epics even when owned by the same team.

- **Scope duplication across sibling epics**: Two or more epics independently build the same data structure, UI surface, or API endpoint. Merge the overlapping epics into one, or re-split along an architectural sub-system boundary (e.g., backend vs. frontend) instead of the current axis. Deduplicate acceptance criteria and scope. Delete any epic files that were merged away and update the decomposition summary.
- **Multi-component/team epic**: Split into separate epics per the component/team tuple rule. Assign new epic IDs continuing the sequence (e.g., if last epic is E007, new ones are E008, E009).
-- **Oversized epic**: Split by sub-deliverable into smaller epics.

+- **Work-type-extracted shared deliverable** (a standalone lint-rule / tooling / validation epic that covers surfaces other implementation epics are converting): fold it back per surface — add the deliverable's slice for each surface to the corresponding epic's Scope and Acceptance Criteria, record the division in the summary's DAG Justification non-edge rationale, delete the extracted epic file and its AI signal file, and update the summary's Epic List, DAG, and `epic_count`.

+- **Oversized epic**: classify first, then apply the matching fix. (a) The overage is a shared-surface deliverable stacked on per-surface work → per-surface fold-back (previous entry). (b) The epic is one logical change over an enumerated surface (a single mechanical sweep) → do NOT split; ensure Health Warnings carry the effort estimate, why the sweep is one logical change, and a concrete conditional re-split trigger (the measurable condition under which it should be re-split) — add the trigger if missing. (c) The epic genuinely bundles multiple logical changes → split by sub-deliverable along the architectural seam, assigning new epic IDs continuing the sequence.
